children: is  reviewing its options after Russia placed the Swiss food company’s local operations under temporary state administration, adding to mounting pressure on Western businesses that still hold assets in the country.
The move was announced in a presidential decree on Thursday. Nestlé

said it was assessing the situation and would take necessary measures to protect its rights while seeking to maintain business continuity, particularly for employees. The company did not disclose what action it may pursue.

operates six factories in Russia producing coffee, pet-care products and infant formula, with about 7,000 employees. Russia generated roughly 2 billion Swiss francs ($2.4 billion) in sales for the group in 2021, the last year Nestlé
reported country-level figures. Analysts estimate its contribution has since fallen to about 1% of group revenue after the company curtailed operations.

The Kremlin has increasingly used temporary administration to gain control over assets owned by companies from countries it considers unfriendly. In some cases, such measures have preceded transfers or sales to Russian buyers.
French retailer Auchan was also targeted by Thursday’s decree.

has defended its remaining Russian operations by citing the importance of food supplies. However, analysts say the latest move could leave the company facing an impairment or an unfavorable disposal of its Russian assets.

title: Nestle faces uncertainty after Russia takes over local operations
